strengths: Addresses a genuinely important practical problem: eliminating the need to collect and label real abnormal video footage, which is costly and constrained by privacy/safety concerns, while still evaluating on the standard weakly-supervised protocol.

The proposed CA-PAG pipeline (CLIP-based class-relevant initial image selection + VLM-driven prompt refinement + I2V diffusion synthesis) is a sensible, well-motivated design that measurably improves generation fidelity and temporal coherence (Table 3, Fig. 6/7), and the qualitative examples (including an honestly reported failure case for 'shoplifting') lend credibility.

The Domain-Aligned Regularized Module is a clear technical contribution that directly targets an identified and empirically demonstrated problem (inflated feature norms/magnitude bias in synthetic anomalies, Table 1) rather than being an ad hoc add-on; its effect is well illustrated with score-trace visualizations (Fig. 8).

Strong and consistent empirical results: PA-VAD with no real abnormal training data reaches 98.2% AUC on ShanghaiTech (beating the strongest real-abnormal WVAD baseline) and 82.5% on UCF-Crime (beating the UVAD SOTA by +1.9), which is a compelling proof of concept.

Thorough ablations (component-wise Table 5, data-scale sensitivity Table 6) and extensive supplementary material (hyperparameters, computational cost, generation examples, failure-case discussion) support reproducibility and transparency.

The paper is honest about its limitations, explicitly noting that it does not surpass real/real WVAD SOTA on UCF-Crime and attributing this to the difficulty of synthesizing long, context-heavy anomalies—this kind of self-critical limitation section strengthens rather than weakens the submission.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to two benchmarks (ShanghaiTech and UCF-Crime); it is unclear how the approach generalizes to other WVAD datasets (e.g., XD-Violence) with different anomaly types, audio-visual content, or scene statistics.

The method depends heavily on large, powerful off-the-shelf components (Wan2.2 I2V-A14B diffusion model, Qwen 30B-A3B VLM, CLIP) whose quality is not ablated—there is no analysis of how sensitive results are to the choice/size of the generator or VLM, making it hard to know how much of the gain is attributable to the proposed pipeline logic versus the strength of the underlying generative backbone.

Generation cost, while framed as 'modest', is still substantial (tens of GPU-hours per dataset on a high-end 100GB GPU) and scales with the number of classes/clips, which could limit practicality for datasets with many fine-grained anomaly categories.

DARM introduces several additional hyperparameters (λ1, λ2, λda, λdist, β) which are only reported as fixed values per dataset; no sensitivity analysis is given, leaving open how much re-tuning would be needed to transfer to new datasets/domains.

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for the AUC numbers, so the reported margins over baselines (e.g., +0.6 on SHT, +1.9 on UCF-Crime UVAD) are not accompanied by an estimate of run-to-run variability.

The self-reported limitation on UCF-Crime (failure to match real/real WVAD SOTA, especially for long, context-heavy anomalies such as shoplifting/abuse) suggests the pseudo-only paradigm may not yet be a full substitute for real data in more complex or temporally extended anomaly categories, somewhat tempering the 'Pseudo Anomalies Are All You Need' framing in the title.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: training video anomaly detectors with zero real abnormal videos, which is highly relevant given privacy/scarcity constraints on collecting real anomalous footage.

The core empirical finding — that diffusion-synthesized pseudo anomalies exhibit a large spatiotemporal feature-magnitude bias that can dominate MIL Top-k selection — is a genuine and well-supported insight (Table 1, Table 5b), and motivates DARM in a principled way rather than as an ad hoc fix.

DARM (domain alignment + usage-aware memory update) is a reasonably simple, interpretable mechanism, and the ablation (Table 5a) and magnitude analysis (Table 5b) convincingly isolate the contribution of each component, showing the usage-aware update is the primary driver while domain alignment adds complementary gains.

Extensive experiments across three standard benchmarks (SHT, UCF-Crime, XD-Violence), with comparisons to UVAD and WVAD baselines, ablations on generator design (init selection, prompt refinement), sensitivity to number of pseudo clips, and open-set generalization experiments (Tables 8-9) that show meaningful gains over OpenVAD, strengthening the significance claim beyond simple closed-set numbers.

The class-aware pseudo-anomaly generation pipeline (CLIP-based initial image selection + VLM prompt refinement) is a thoughtful, well-motivated design that is shown via ablation and qualitative examples (Fig. 6, Table 3) to meaningfully improve fidelity and downstream detection performance over naive prompting.

The paper is transparent about a genuine limitation (UCF-Crime performance gap to real-abnormal WVAD SOTA) and offers a plausible explanation (difficulty of synthesizing long, context-heavy anomalies), which strengthens rather than undermines the overall claims.
Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed supplementary material with hyperparameters, VLM/CLIP prompts, generation settings, and computational cost breakdown.
weaknesses: The framework substitutes real abnormal video collection with heavy reliance on large pretrained generative (Wan2.2) and vision-language (Qwen3, Qwen2.5-VL, CLIP) models; the paper does not discuss whether these pretrained priors may have been exposed to similar surveillance/anomaly content during their own training, which could constitute an indirect form of data leakage not accounted for in the 'no real abnormal data' framing.

Table 4's cross-method comparison has many missing entries (dashes) for baselines across datasets, making some of the headline comparisons (e.g., surpassing WVAD SOTA on SHT/XD) less comprehensive than the abstract's framing suggests; a fully aligned comparison table with consistent baselines per dataset would strengthen the claims.

No variance/multiple-seed reporting for the main results in Table 4 (only open-set experiments in Tables 8-9 report standard deviation), leaving uncertainty about the robustness/stability of the headline AUC numbers.

The domain-alignment component operates only on real/pseudo-normal streams rather than directly on abnormal features, and the ablation shows it provides only modest benefit alone; its theoretical justification for correcting bias on the abnormal side (which is where the actual problem lies, per Table 5b) is somewhat indirect and could be better motivated or replaced/compared with a more direct alternative.

Generation quality evaluation relies solely on standard automated metrics (FID/KID/FVD/KVD) and qualitative visual examples; no human evaluation of surveillance-realism or a systematic characterization of failure modes across all anomaly classes (only one failure case—shoplifting—is discussed) is provided, which limits confidence in the general fidelity of the synthesis pipeline.

The method involves nontrivial manual engineering of positive/negative CLIP phrases and VLM refinement instructions per class/dataset, which somewhat undercuts the claim of removing manual prompt search, and raises questions about how much tuning effort would be needed to extend to new domains or anomaly classes.

No ablation on the choice of the underlying video diffusion/VLM models (e.g., substituting Stable Video Diffusion or a different VLM) is provided, so it is unclear how sensitive the pipeline's success is to the specific choice of Wan2.2/Qwen models used.
